bank.prompt: After Re8+ Black has exactly one legal move on the board. Tap the square his queen must go to.
bank.reason: Qf8 blocks. The king has no square, his own pawns cover f7, g7 and h7, and nothing black reaches e8.

bank.prompt: Play the whole idea: the check, his forced answer, the rook, and then the knight you came for.
bank.reason: Five ply and Black never had a choice. A queen for a rook, and the knight on h1 as well. Kxh1 at once wins a knight and leaves the game level.

bank.prompt: Two of your pieces can take the knight on d8. Your first rank is bare. Take it with the right one.
bank.reason: Rxd8+ Rxd8 Nxd8 wins the piece. Nxd8 first loses to Rb1+ Rd1 Rxd1 mate, because it is not check.

bank.prompt: You play Rxd8, taking the knight with check. Is the rook safe on d8?
reasons: Yes. The check means Black has to move his king and cannot take.
Yes. Nothing black is left that can reach d8.
No. Rxd8 is his only legal move, and then your knight takes the rook back.
bank.reason: It can be taken, and being taken is the plan: Rxd8 is forced and Nxd8 leaves you a piece up with his first rank never used.

bank.prompt: His knight on d3 is hanging and your queen can take it. Look at your own first rank before you do.
bank.reason: Qxd3 at once loses to Qe1+ Qf1 Qxf1 mate. Ra8+ has four answers and none of them is Qe1.

bank.prompt: The pawn on f7 is there for the taking. Check the order before you take anything.
bank.reason: Rxf7 at once is met by Qe1 mate. Rc8+ comes first and Qf8 is his only legal answer to it.

bank.prompt: Two captures are available and both of them are losing moves. Find the one move that is not.
bank.reason: Rxa3 and Rxf7 both allow Qe1 mate. Rd8+ is check, Qf8 is forced, and only then is there time for anything else.

bank.prompt: His knight on d6 is loose and your queen can have it. Count his answer before you take.
bank.reason: Qxd6 is met by Qe1 mate. Qd8+ first, and he has two blocks and no time for the first rank.

bank.prompt: Your knight on a4 is hanging. Leave it there and give him something worse to think about.
bank.reason: Rc8 threatens Rxd8 mate. Every knight move leaves the game level; Qxa4 loses to Rxd8+ Qe8 Rxe8 mate.

bank.prompt: Find out what is actually under fire before you decide anything. Tap every white man Black attacks.
bank.reason: The queen on a2 hits the knight up the a-file and the pawn on f2 along the second rank. The pawn has the king behind it; the knight has nothing.

bank.prompt: He takes the knight anyway. Show him the bill: the rook, his only answer, and the finish.
bank.reason: After Rxd8+ the block on e8 is his only legal move, and Rxe8 is mate. A knight for the game.

bank.prompt: The rook is attacked twice and the queen once, and you have one move. Move the rook somewhere useful.
bank.reason: Rb5 saves the rook and adds a second attacker on the knight on b3. The queen stays on b1 because Bxb1 loses to Rb8+ and mate.

bank.prompt: You move the rook to b5. Run the check on it: is the rook safe there?
reasons: Yes. Nothing black attacks b5 at all. His queen sees b3 down the diagonal, not b5.
No. The knight on b3 takes it.
No. His queen on e6 covers b5 from the diagonal.
bank.reason: Safe, and doing two jobs: off the two attacks on f5, and on to the knight. The diagonal from e6 runs to b3, one square short of b5.

bank.prompt: His bishop on c2 is attacking your rook on d1 and nothing defends it. Do not move the rook.
bank.reason: Nf6+ is check, so the rook can wait. The best rook move is worth about a pawn; the check is worth six times that.

bank.prompt: His knight on g3 is attacking your queen and nothing defends her. Find something better than moving her.
bank.reason: Ne7+ is check and Kf8 is his only legal answer. Qf5 instead loses to Qe1 mate, and Qd1 leaves the game level.

bank.prompt: The knight on a3 is attacking your queen on b5. Why is Ne7 the move rather than moving her?
options: Because the queen on b5 is defended, so taking her would cost him material.
Because Ne7 is check. He has to answer it, and the two queen retreats Qd5 and Qe5 are both mated in two.
Because the knight on e7 covers b5 from its new square, so she is defended after all.
bank.reason: Nothing white defends b5. A knight on e7 covers c6, c8, d5, f5, g6 and g8, not b5. What makes Ne7 work is that it is check and he has only two king moves.

bank.prompt: In check on the first rank. Two pieces can get in the way, and one of them is being attacked already.
bank.reason: Qe1 gets in the way and leaves the third rank at once. Re1 allows Rxc3 bxc3, a queen for a rook.

bank.prompt: Three legal moves and all three get in the way of the check. Play the one that is still there next move.
bank.reason: Nb1 is the only one your queen on e4 defends. Rxb1 Qxb1 and the game goes on; Qe1 is met by Rxe1 mate.

bank.prompt: In check along the first rank with no king move available. Tap every square you can put a piece on.
bank.reason: b1 and e1. The knight reaches b1 and the queen reaches both, which is the whole of your legal move list.

bank.prompt: Check on the first rank, three ways to get in the way. One of your pieces is loose where it stands.
bank.reason: The knight on d3 has nothing defending it. Nc1 gets in the way and takes it off that square, and the bishop on e3 defends c1. Bc1 instead allows Rd8 and the knight drops.

bank.prompt: Four legal moves and every one of them gets in the way. Pick the piece that can afford to stand there.
bank.reason: Nf1 is the cheapest of the four and it is covered twice, by the queen on d3 and by the king. Blocking with the queen simply loses her to the rook.

bank.prompt: Four ways to answer this check and all four are the same kind of move. So how do you choose?
options: By what stands on the square afterwards. His rook takes whatever you put there, so put the cheapest piece you have that something of yours defends.
By which square is furthest from his rook, since that buys you the most time.
By which one also gives check back, because a check always comes first.
bank.reason: Getting in the way hands him a capture and you cannot avoid that. What you choose is the price. None of the four is a check, so the third answer is not even on offer.

bank.prompt: Two legal moves, both on the same square, both defended. Choose.
bank.reason: Both blocks are covered, so it comes down to price: Bd1 Rxd1 Rxd1 gets a rook for a bishop, while Rd1 Rxd1 Bxd1 is only rook for rook.

bank.prompt: Two squares to get in the way on, and only one of them has anything looking after it.
bank.reason: Your king covers f1 and nothing at all covers d1. Rxf1 Kxf1 and the check is over; Bd1 just loses a bishop.

bank.prompt: The knight on h4 is attacked, undefended, and every square it can reach is covered. Stop trying to keep it.
bank.reason: Nxf5 and he takes back with the bishop or the queen. Ng6 hands the knight to a pawn; this is the move that gets a rook for it.

bank.prompt: Your knight on h4 has three squares. Tap every black man that covers at least one of them.
bank.reason: The queen on g4 covers all three. The bishop on d3 and the rook on f5 add f5 and f3, and the pawns on f7 and h7 add g6. Five men, nowhere to go.

bank.prompt: The knight is going. Get a rook for it and then hold the position together for eight moves.
bank.reason: Nxf5 first, and after the recapture the game is level. The knight was never the thing to save; the balance was.

bank.prompt: You are worse whatever you play, and the knight on b7 has no square his queen does not cover. Get something for it.
bank.reason: Nxd8 Qxd8 is a rook better than any retreat. Nc5 and Na5 are both mated by Rd1+ Qe1 Rxe1.

bank.prompt: You try to bring the knight home with Nd6. Is it safe on d6?
reasons: Yes. The bishop on h8 covers d6 along the long diagonal.
No. His queen on c7 takes it, and so does the rook on d8.
Yes. His queen has to stay where she is to hold the rook on d8.
bank.reason: Two attackers and no defenders. Your bishop on h8 has one square, g7, because his pawn blocks the diagonal. Every square that knight can reach is covered by the queen alone.

bank.prompt: One black piece covers your knight on b7 and every square it could move to. Tap the square that piece stands on.
bank.reason: The queen on c7. She holds b7 where it stands and d8, d6, c5 and a5 as well, so there is no escape to find and nothing to look for but the biggest capture.

bank.prompt: His own king is attacking your knight on f8, and all four of its squares are covered. Pick the expensive one.
bank.reason: Nxd7 takes a rook and Rxd7 answers. Ne6 looks free until you notice the pawn on f7 takes there, and Ng6 and Nxh7 give the knight away for a pawn at most.

bank.prompt: Both your rooks are attacked and both can take the bishop on e6. Take with the right one.
bank.reason: The rook on h6 is the one with nowhere to go, so it is the one that spends itself. Take with the e2 rook instead and the h6 rook is still attacked by the pawn on g7.

bank.prompt: Black has no check and no capture anywhere, and his bishop is one quiet move from your rook on d3, from either side.
bank.reason: Rfd1 defends d3 from behind, so Bb5 Bxd3 is met by Rxd3. You cannot stop him reaching b5 or f5 and you do not need to.

bank.prompt: His checks and his captures come back empty. Tap every square his bishop on d7 can reach that attacks your rook on d3.
bank.reason: b5 and f5, out of nine squares. Neither is a check and neither is a capture, so a scan of his forcing moves would never have shown them.

bank.prompt: No checks and no captures for him, and three squares on the sixth rank that all lead to mate. You get one move.
bank.reason: Rc4 sits on the file he wants most, so Rc6 is simply met by Rxc6. A quiet move answering a quiet move.

bank.prompt: Tap every square his rook on a6 can reach from which he would have mate on the move after.
bank.reason: c6, d6 and e6, with Rc1, Rd1 and Re1 all mate. b6 is blocked by your rook on b3, f6 by the pawn on f2, g6 by your rook on g4 and h6 by the pawn on h2.

bank.prompt: Nothing forcing is available to him at all. Tap the one square his bishop wants.
bank.reason: g6, the only one of its five squares that joins the diagonal running down to your queen on b1, which nothing defends.

bank.prompt: His knight has two squares that both hit your rook on c2, and nothing defends it. Move the rook somewhere useful.
bank.reason: Rc5 leaves the fork and attacks the bishop on a5, so he is the one answering a threat. Nothing black reaches c5.

bank.prompt: You move the rook to c5, hitting the bishop. Is the rook safe on c5?
reasons: No. The knight on f5 covers c5.
No. His rook on b8 comes to b5 and takes it.
Yes. Nothing black attacks c5 at all, and the bishop on a5 does not cover it either.
bank.reason: Safe. The knight reaches d6, e7, h6, h4, g3, e3 and d4, and c5 is on none of them. He has to answer the threat to the bishop instead of making one of his own.

bank.prompt: No checks and no captures for Black, and your rook on e2 has nothing defending it. Find what his knight is about to do.
bank.reason: Nd4 comes next and Nxe2 wins the rook. Rfe1 puts a second rook behind the first, so Nd4 Nxe2 is answered by Rxe2.
